title: HBM-free near-memory accelerators gain a second Chinese entrant by H2 2027
body: Dongfang Suanxin's DF1000 — a 14nm, HBM-free accelerator that leans on 3D-stacked near-memory computing to claim 6.4 TB/s of bandwidth, roughly a third more than an H200, while conceding about half its raw BF16 compute — is the first clean proof that a bandwidth-first, packaging-driven design can route around the two binding US export chokepoints at once: leading-edge lithography and HBM. With more than ten domestic compute-chip vendors already exhibiting general-purpose accelerators at WAIC, the architecture is unlikely to stay a single-vendor curiosity. As the DF1000 moves toward its targeted end-2026 mass production and a promised 2x DF2000 follow-on, expect at least one additional Chinese vendor to announce or tape out a comparable HBM-free, near-memory part that trades peak FLOPS for memory bandwidth — turning near-memory computing plus advanced packaging into a replicated domestic template rather than a one-off, and giving buyers a second independent data point on whether the bandwidth claims survive real workloads.

summary: Dongfang Suanxin's HBM-free 14nm DF1000 claims 6.4 TB/s — ~33% above an H200 — via 3D near-memory computing, not HBM. With 10+ domestic accelerator vendors at WAIC, expect a second Chinese HBM-free, bandwidth-first part by H2 2027, making the design a replicated export-control workaround.
